item.title: Witkoff says U.S. demands any Iran nuclear deal last indefinitely
item.description:
U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff told a private gathering of AIPAC donors in Washington on Tuesday that the Trump administration is insisting any nuclear deal with Iran include no sunset clause, according to a report by Axios citing a U.S. official and two other people familiar with his remarks.

"We go to the Iranians with the understanding that there will be no sunset provision," Witkoff said, according to Axios. "Regardless of whether a deal is achieved, our position is clear: you must adhere to these terms for life."

The demand, made just two days before the next round of U.S.-Iran talks scheduled for Thursday in Geneva, marks a direct attempt to address what President Trump and other critics have long called the central flaw of the 2015 nuclear agreement brokered by the Obama administration. Under that deal, known as the JCPOA, most restrictions on Iran's nuclear activities were set to expire between eight and 25 years after signing.

item.title: Trump speaks with Zelenskyy as Geneva talks set for Thursday
item.description: President Donald Trump spoke by phone with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on Wednesday, Axios reported, as the two sides work to lay the groundwork for a fresh round of trilateral negotiations with Russia expected in early March. The call came one day after Trump told Congress that his administration is "working very hard" to end the war in Ukraine, where he said "25,000 soldiers are dying each and every month."

item.title: Cuba kills four on Florida speedboat in firefight
item.description: Cuba's coast guard shot dead four people and injured six others aboard a U.S.-registered speedboat in an exchange of fire off the island's northern coast on Wednesday morning, the country's Interior Ministry said. The deadly confrontation comes amid a period of intense friction between Washington and Havana over a U.S.-backed oil embargo that has crippled the Cuban economy.

item.title: Spanish scientists build solar panel that also harvests rain energy
item.description: A team of scientists in Seville has created a hybrid device that generates electricity from sunlight and rain simultaneously, turning one of renewable energy's persistent headaches — bad weather — into an additional power source. The work, published in the journal Nano Energy, introduces a thin protective film that shields fragile perovskite solar cells from moisture while also converting the kinetic energy of falling raindrops into electric current.

item.title: AI models used nuclear weapons in 95% of war games, study finds
item.description:
Leading AI systems from OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google chose to deploy nuclear weapons in 20 of 21 simulated geopolitical crises, according to new research from King's College London that raises pointed questions about the role of artificial intelligence in military decision-making.

The study, authored by Kenneth Payne and published on the preprint server arXiv on February 16, tested three frontier large language models — OpenAI's GPT-5.2, Anthropic's Claude Sonnet 4, and Google's Gemini 3 Flash — in a series of war games involving territorial disputes, competition over scarce resources, and regime survival scenarios. Over 329 turns across the 21 games, the models generated roughly 780,000 words of strategic reasoning. In none of the simulations did any model choose to surrender or fully accommodate its adversary.

"The nuclear taboo doesn't seem to be as powerful for machines as for humans," Payne told New Scientist.

item.title: DeepSeek shuts out Nvidia, AMD from new AI model
item.description:
Chinese artificial intelligence lab DeepSeek has broken with standard industry practice by excluding American chipmakers, including Nvidia and AMD, from early access to its upcoming flagship V4 model, according to a Reuters exclusive citing two sources familiar with the matter.

Instead, DeepSeek granted domestic suppliers, including Huawei Technologies, a head start of several weeks to optimize software for their processors ahead of the model's expected release.

item.title: Canada, South Korea sign military intel-sharing pact
item.description:
Canada and South Korea signed a defense agreement on Wednesday focused on the exchange and protection of classified military information, as Ottawa looks to deepen ties with like-minded middle powers and Seoul positions itself to win a multibillion-dollar Canadian submarine contract.

The signing took place during the second Canada-Republic of Korea Foreign and Defence (2+2) Ministerial Meeting in Ottawa, where Canadian Defence Minister David McGuinty and Foreign Affairs Minister Anita Anand met with their South Korean counterparts, Defence Minister Ahn Gyuback and Foreign Minister Cho Hyun.

item.title: Tropical flowers blooming weeks later due to climate change, study finds
item.description:
Tropical plants are flowering weeks or even months earlier or later than they once did as a result of climate change, according to a study of more than 8,000 plant specimens collected over two centuries. The findings, published on February 25, 2026 in the journal PLOS One, challenge the long-held assumption that tropical ecosystems — home to more than half the world's plant biodiversity — are insulated from the phenological disruptions already documented in temperate and boreal regions.

Researchers Skylar Graves and Erin Manzitto-Tripp of the University of Colorado-Boulder analyzed museum herbarium specimens representing 33 tropical species with distinct annual flowering periods, collected between 1794 and 2024 from sites in Brazil, Ecuador, Peru, Ghana, Guinea, Thailand, and Bolivia. They found that flowering periods have shifted by an average of about two days per decade.

item.title: Nvidia's record Q4 earnings send Asian markets to new highs
item.description:
Asian stock markets rallied on Thursday after Nvidia reported record fourth-quarter revenue that handily topped Wall Street forecasts, easing concerns about the sustainability of the artificial intelligence boom. US and European futures, however, drifted lower as investors weighed the chipmaker's results alongside lingering trade-policy uncertainty.

Nvidia posted quarterly revenue of $68.1 billion for the three months ending January 25, a 73% jump from the year-ago period and roughly $2 billion above analysts' consensus estimates. Non-GAAP earnings per share came in at $1.62, beating expectations of around $1.53. The company also guided for $78 billion in first-quarter revenue, well ahead of the approximately $72 billion Wall Street had penciled in.

"Computing demand is growing exponentially — the agentic AI inflection point has arrived," CEO Jensen Huang said in a statement, adding that customers "are racing to invest in AI compute". On the earnings call, Huang declared that "AI is here, AI is not going to go back".

item.title: UN issues first carbon credits under Paris Agreement
item.description:
The United Nations on Thursday approved the first-ever carbon credits under the global carbon market established by the Paris Agreement, a milestone for international climate finance that has been more than a decade in the making — and one that has already drawn scrutiny from environmental watchdogs.

The approved credits stem from a clean-cooking project in Myanmar that distributes efficient wood-burning cookstoves to reduce household air pollution and ease pressure on local forests, the UNFCCC announced in a press release. The project, coordinated with a South Korean company, will generate credits counting toward the climate targets of both South Korea and Myanmar.

item.title: Scripps Research finds hidden structure in cell droplets, opening new drug targets
item.description: Scientists at Scripps Research have upended a long-standing assumption in cell biology by discovering that some biomolecular condensates — the membrane-less, droplet-like compartments that cells use to organize essential processes — contain intricate internal networks of protein filaments. The findings, published in Nature Structural & Molecular Biology, point to new therapeutic possibilities for diseases including cancer and neurodegeneration.

item.title: Oil holds near 7-month highs as US-Iran talks open in Geneva
item.description:
Oil prices edged higher on Thursday, hovering near seven-month highs, as investors weighed whether a third round of nuclear talks between the United States and Iran could avert a military confrontation that threatens to disrupt crude supplies from the Middle East.

Brent crude futures traded near $71 a barrel, while West Texas Intermediate held around $65.50, both largely flat after settling with minimal changes on Wednesday, according to Reuters. Brent had earlier in the week reached its highest level since late July as Washington continued to position military forces in the region to pressure Tehran into a deal.

item.title: Rutgers study challenges theory that melting glaciers could slow climate change
item.description:
Marine scientists at Rutgers University have found that meltwater from an Antarctic ice shelf delivers far less iron to the surrounding ocean than long assumed, upending a widely held theory that glacier-driven iron fertilization could act as a natural brake on climate change. The findings were published Tuesday in the journal Communications Earth and Environment.

The theory posits that as rising temperatures cause Antarctic glaciers to melt, the iron released would nourish blooms of microscopic algae in the Southern Ocean. Those algae absorb carbon dioxide as they grow, theoretically pulling heat-trapping gas from the atmosphere. But direct sampling beneath the Dotson Ice Shelf in West Antarctica's Amundsen Sea has shown the mechanism is far weaker than models predicted.

item.title: Ivory Coast to slash cocoa farmer prices in historic move
item.description:
Ivory Coast, the world's largest cocoa producer, will bring forward the start of its cocoa mid-crop season for the first time in history and sharply reduce prices paid to farmers, according to two government sources and two regulatory sources who spoke to Reuters. The move is designed to help the West African nation clear a growing pile of unsold cocoa that has accumulated at ports and inland storage sites in recent months.

Under the plan, cocoa harvested beginning in March will be classified as mid-crop rather than main crop, with the farmer price set at between 800 and 1,000 CFA francs ($1.45 to $1.81) per kilogram — a steep drop from the current main crop rate of 2,800 CFA francs. The mid-crop traditionally begins in April and runs through September, but it will now start on March 1 and end a month earlier, in late August. The changes were approved by an interministerial committee overseeing raw materials last week.

item.title: Flinders University scientists develop nano-cage that removes 98% of PFAS from water
item.description:
Researchers at Flinders University in South Australia have developed a nano-sized molecular cage that can remove more than 98 percent of toxic "forever chemicals" from tap water, offering a potential breakthrough in tackling one of the most persistent forms of water contamination worldwide.

The study, published in the journal Angewandte Chemie International Edition, details how the team led by Dr. Witold Bloch engineered a molecular cage that acts as a highly selective trap for per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances, known as PFAS. The method is notable for its ability to capture short-chain PFAS — smaller, more water-soluble variants that have long eluded conventional water treatment technologies.

item.title: Invasive species, drought threaten water on 3 continents
item.description: From dried-up lakes in southern India to a deepening water crisis across Türkiye and aging infrastructure in the U.S. Midwest, a convergence of invasive species, drought, and extreme weather is threatening water and food supplies across three continents. New research, government warnings, and expert testimony this week underscored the urgency of the challenges facing billions of people who depend on increasingly fragile water systems.

item.title: Magnetic microrobot swarms move objects without touching them
item.description:
Swarms of tiny magnetic robots can now rotate, transport, and assemble objects thousands of times their own mass — all without making physical contact. In a study published this week in Science Advances, researchers from the Max Planck Institute for Intelligent Systems, the University of Michigan, and Cornell University demonstrated that coordinated groups of spinning microrobots generate controllable fluid flows powerful enough to manipulate passive objects from a distance.

The technique, which the team calls fluidic torque-enabled manipulation, works by spinning disk-shaped microrobots — each roughly 300 micrometers in diameter — under an externally applied magnetic field. As the disks rotate in a liquid, they create circular flow patterns that exert torque on nearby objects. By adjusting the spin rate, the number of robots, and their spatial arrangement, the researchers tuned the generated torque to levels as high as 3.6 × 10⁻⁹ newton-meters.

item.title: US and Iran hold critical nuclear talks as Trump's deadline nears
item.description:
Iran and the United States are set to hold a third round of indirect nuclear negotiations in Geneva on Thursday, in what both sides and outside observers describe as a last-ditch diplomatic effort to prevent a military confrontation. The talks come amid a massive American military buildup in the Middle East and just days before a deadline set by President Donald Trump for Tehran to accept a deal on its nuclear program.

Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi, who arrived in Geneva on Wednesday night, will lead Iran's delegation, while White House envoy Steve Witkoff and Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner will represent the American side. As in prior rounds, Oman's Foreign Minister Badr al-Busaidi is serving as an intermediary, shuttling proposals between the two delegations, which are not meeting face to face.

item.title: US, Ukraine meet in Geneva after Russia's massive overnight aerial barrage
item.description:
Ukraine's lead negotiator Rustem Umerov was set to meet US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner in Geneva on Thursday for bilateral talks focused on Ukraine's postwar economic recovery and preparations for a new round of trilateral negotiations with Russia expected in early March. The meeting came just hours after Russia launched one of its largest aerial assaults in months, firing 420 drones and 39 missiles at targets across eight Ukrainian regions overnight.

The Geneva session marks the latest effort by the Trump administration to maintain diplomatic momentum as the war enters its fifth year, with both sides still deadlocked over the fate of Russian-occupied Ukrainian territory.

item.title: NASA-backed study turns recycled sewage into lunar and Martian crop fertilizer
item.description:
Researchers working with NASA have demonstrated that recycled human and plant waste can be combined with simulated lunar and Martian soil to release nutrients essential for growing crops, a step toward making off-world agriculture sustainable for future space colonies.

The study, published in ACS Earth and Space Chemistry and highlighted in a press release this week by the American Chemical Society, describes how a nutrient-dense solution derived from processed sewage was mixed with materials designed to mimic the rocky, barren surfaces of the moon and Mars. The interaction released plant-essential elements including sulfur, calcium, and magnesium, offering early evidence that waste recycling could transform lifeless extraterrestrial terrain into something approaching farmable soil.
